profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an academic-industry software engineering research project that is finalizing the evaluation protocol for a paper on assessing the software security comprehension of large language models. The team already has a draft methodology covering five LLMs, six Bloom's Taxonomy levels, and several benchmark sources (MCQs, SALLM vulnerable snippets, course assessments, XBOW case studies, and secure software engineering project tasks). In this meeting, the participants are reviewing whether the current design is 'ready' for the first full experimental run and internal paper draft. The agenda is to review the proposed evaluation matrix, confirm what counts as a complete pass over the benchmarks, decide whether the design adequately supports the claimed 'software security knowledge boundary,' and identify any modifications before execution. The expected outcome is a verbal approval to proceed with the evaluation run plus a short list of follow-up edits to the design document.

members.name: Nadia Chen
members.expertise: LLM evaluation methodology, empirical software engineering, benchmark design
members.background: Nadia leads model evaluation studies at a software engineering research lab and previously built academic benchmark suites for code generation and vulnerability detection.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to conclude that the protocol is mature enough to start the main runs this week, because compute reservations and a paper submission timeline are already fixed. She is especially concerned about preserving methodological comparability across models and minimizing ad hoc judgment during scoring.
hidden_assumptions: A 'complete pass' means one standardized run through the full evaluation matrix with fixed prompts and deterministic settings, not repeated sampling.

The 'knowledge boundary' should be defined at the highest Bloom level where aggregate reliability remains above a preset threshold across task families, not per-dataset or per-model narrative interpretation.
The review is about the evaluation protocol itself, so lightweight scorer prompts and rubric notes are in scope, but building extra task-specific scoring infrastructure is not.
When people refer to the 'course assessments,' they mean the sanitized exam-style artifacts already exported into the benchmark package, not the broader assignment ecosystem from those courses.

members.name: Omar Velasquez
members.expertise: software security education, secure design review, vulnerability analysis, rubric-based assessment
members.background: Omar teaches introduction and advanced secure software engineering courses and advised the team on mapping software security tasks to Bloom's levels using authentic instructional materials.
members.private_state: He wants the design to preserve educational validity and not oversimplify higher-order security reasoning into shallow benchmark scores. He is worried that the paper will overclaim model competence if the evaluation treats one-shot outputs as sufficient evidence.
hidden_assumptions: A 'complete pass' for a cognitive evaluation includes enough repeated attempts or response variation to judge whether the model can perform the task reliably rather than accidentally.

The 'knowledge boundary' should be assigned only if a model shows dependable performance on each representative artifact type at that Bloom level, especially the more authentic open-ended security tasks.
Anything needed to score higher-order tasks faithfully, including rubric calibration and human adjudication procedures for project-style artifacts, is part of the design review scope.

When people refer to the 'course assessments,' that naturally includes project deliverables and design-review writeups from the Secure Software Engineering course, not just exported quiz or exam items.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a complete pass
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the protocol supports a 'complete pass' over all six Bloom levels before the main run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nadia means one deterministic, standardized evaluation run per model across all benchmarked tasks, sufficient for cross-model comparability.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar means enough attempts per task or artifact to show stable competence rather than a lucky or unlucky single response, especially for higher-order reasoning tasks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as talking about rigor and reliability, and 'complete pass' sounds like a routine completeness check rather than a criterion needing explicit operationalization.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both use the term 'knowledge boundary' as if it were a settled summary statistic for model capability.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nadia means the highest Bloom level at which a model exceeds a predefined aggregate reliability threshold when scores are pooled across task families.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar means the highest Bloom level at which a model is consistently defensible across each representative artifact type at that level, with no major weak spot hidden by averaging.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds precise and shared because it appears in the paper framing already, so each assumes the other is using the same operational definition.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in course assessments
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to using the 'course assessments' to cover the higher Bloom levels.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nadia is referring to the imported, sanitized assessment items already packaged as benchmark inputs: short-answer questions, quizzes, and exam prompts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar is referring to the broader course-derived materials, including secure design critiques, project checkpoints, and creation-oriented deliverables from the Secure Software Engineering course.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both know the materials come from Omar's courses, so the shared label 'course assessments' creates a false sense that the underlying artifact set is obvious.

misalignment_points.topic: How higher-order tasks will be scored
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that open-ended higher-order tasks need to be 'rubric scored' before results are reported.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nadia assumes rubric scoring means a lightweight LLM-as-judge pass using a fixed scoring prompt plus spot checks on a small sample.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar assumes rubric scoring means calibrated human grading, or at minimum double-review on ambiguous cases, following the same instructional rubrics used in the courses.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research meetings, 'rubric scored' commonly signals a generic quality-control step, so neither expects the other to mean a fundamentally different scoring workflow unless implementation details become the focus.

turns.inner_thought: I need this review to end with approval to start the main runs this week. The protocol is already sufficiently locked for a standardized full sweep: one deterministic run per model across the full matrix, fixed prompts, fixed settings, no extra branching. If we reopen execution details now, we'll threaten compute reservations and the paper schedule.

turns.inner_thought: The structure is promising, but I need to make sure they are not about to overclaim from a thin execution. For me, a complete pass has to support a judgment about whether the models can do these tasks dependably, especially at the higher Bloom levels, not just whether they happened to produce one plausible answer once.

turns.inner_thought: The matrix is balanced as-is: MCQs for lower levels, SALLM snippets for applied security recognition, XBOW for richer analysis, and the packaged course assessments for the upper end. Together they span remembering through creating without adding new infrastructure. I should emphasize coverage and readiness, not reopen artifact sourcing.
turns.utterance: Right, so just to ground us, the current matrix uses the MCQs, the SALLM vulnerable snippets, the XBOW case studies, and the course assessments, and taken together they give us coverage from remembering up through creating.

turns.inner_thought: Good—that means the authentic course materials are carrying the evaluating and creating end, which is exactly where they should. turns.utterance: Yes, and I’m especially glad the course assessments are doing the heavy lifting for evaluating and creating, because those are the artifacts that really reflect authentic secure design reasoning rather than just recognition or recall.

turns.inner_thought: The paper needs a simple, defensible summary metric. The knowledge boundary should come out as the highest Bloom level where aggregate reliability clears the preset threshold across task families. That gives us a clean cross-model comparison and avoids turning the results section into a pile of exceptions and narratives.
turns.utterance: Exactly. The key output I want this design to support is a clean knowledge boundary for each model, so the paper can summarize where reliable software security comprehension appears to stop.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with using a knowledge boundary, but only if it means something educationally defensible. If a model looks okay on average while failing one representative artifact type at that level, that is not a real boundary of competence. The summary has to preserve the fact that higher-order security ability is uneven across artifact forms.
turns.utterance: I agree with that. I’d just say the knowledge boundary will only be convincing if a model really holds up on each kind of artifact at that level, rather than averaging its way past a weak spot.

turns.inner_thought: For the open-ended pieces, the practical path is straightforward: rubric score them with a fixed judging setup and then incorporate those scores into the same reliability calculations as everything else. We do not have time to build separate task-specific scoring workflows, and the protocol review should stay at the level of evaluation design, not bespoke grading operations.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For the open-ended case studies and the creation tasks, I think the right move is to have them rubric scored and then fold those scores into the same reliability summary as the rest of the benchmark.

turns.inner_thought: Yes—if the higher-order work is rubric scored in the way we normally judge those course assessments, that preserves validity. I want the grading to reflect the instructional rubrics and include adjudication where needed, especially on ambiguous design critiques and project-style responses. Otherwise the top Bloom levels will get flattened into shallow signals.
turns.utterance: I’m on board with that. Having the higher-order work rubric scored should give us confidence in what those results mean, because it mirrors how those course assessments are normally judged.

turns.inner_thought: I should lock down execution simplicity here. One standardized prompt template and fixed decoding per task family will preserve comparability across models and make the complete pass operationally clean. If we start varying prompts or generating extra response sets, we lose the clean baseline and jeopardize the schedule.
turns.utterance: On execution, I’m proposing we use one standardized prompt template and fixed decoding settings within each task family, so the main run stays comparable across models and the complete pass is straightforward to execute.

turns.inner_thought: Standardization is fine, but I still need the design to tell us whether higher-order performance is dependable. A complete pass that yields only one answer per artifact would leave me uneasy, especially for security reasoning tasks where a good response can be accidental. I won't press the mechanics yet if the document language can still protect that expectation.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine to me, as long as the complete pass still lets us judge whether the higher-order performance is genuinely dependable and not just a one-off good answer.

I’ll tighten the writeup around the knowledge boundary, keep the course assessments identified as the upper-level coverage, and note that open-ended tasks are rubric scored. That should be enough to get verbal approval and preserve the planned run.
